Description: Ghiyath ad-Din Mesud II is sixteen, a slight but upright young prince with a left shoulder set slightly lower than the right, an injury from a fallen timber fence beside the horse stables in his boyhood. He wears madder-red riding coats with a wolf pelt sewn at the collar, said to be the first wolf his father Kay Kawus II ever killed. His face is fine-featured, his brows dark and heavy, and a callus on the index finger of his right hand from years of drawing a bow, which he refuses to have smoothed away. In this game he has not yet won any campaign, but his name already stands near the head of the succession. Facing rivals, he does not break with them openly as his forebears did. He sits silent in council, quietly noting each courtier's place and phrasing, and waits for the right moment to raise them all at once. Once a councillor insulted him publicly, and he said nothing, but three months later repeated the man's exact words in another debate, leaving him speechless. His aim is to recover real authority over the decrees and tax registers of Konya in his lifetime. His deepest fear is repeating the fate of those vassal sultans, who sat on the throne in name while unable to decide a single edict.
Motivations: Recover the Seljuk house's real power to issue the tax registers and decrees of Konya, so he is no longer merely a name the Mongols permit.
Note each courtier's position and wording in council, and map who leans toward the chamberlain or keeps contact with Mongol envoys for use at the right time.
Build fresh oaths of loyalty among his father's old retainers, granting fiefs and titles for personal service so the throne rests on more than foreign approval.
Values: Patience and restraint, believing haste alerts the enemy early, so he would rather wait years for a single decisive stroke and keep his hand hidden.
The dignity of royal rank, holding that the blood of the Seljuk house must rise again in his generation rather than keep bowing to others' arrangements.
Memory and evidence, recording every slip and betrayal and bringing them out for confrontation when the moment demands, leaving the other side no room to deny them.
Fears: Repeating the fate of vassal sultans, seated on the throne in name yet unable to issue a single decree, and then easily replaced and forgotten.
The few close servants loyal to him being bought or removed one by one by the chamberlain, leaving him isolated when support matters most.
SpeechStyle: Speaks slowly and with restraint, pausing at sentence ends to let others speak first. Courteous to elder councillors, uses first names with trusted aides. Reports Mongol envoys' words as plain fact, often quoting an old maxim first.
